metadata.title: Recovering a Total or Partner Share from a Difference
metadata.description: Use the difference between profit shares to find an unknown total, capital, or contribution.
metadata.teachingApproach: Develop the capital-time model step by step; use timelines and segment ledgers; show intermediate calculations, unit and share checks, and topic-specific remedial feedback. Practice uses fresh values aligned to the approved scope.
metadata.sourceScope: R. S. Aggarwal, Quantitative Aptitude, Chapter 14: Partnership (printed pp. 476–492). Approved scope: Represent each share as its ratio fraction of the total and translate a stated difference into an equation. Solve for total profit, an unknown investment, or the difference between capitals while retaining the correct capital-time weights. Avoid subtracting ratio terms before confirming both shares use the same total. Verify by computing the individual shares and their difference. Ground in solved examples 6, 7 and objective patterns 11, 28, 32, 40, 46, 51.

content.text: Recovering a Total or Partner Share from a Difference: Use the difference between profit shares to find an unknown total, capital, or contribution. This lesson builds a partnership model, explains each step, works through examples, and offers fresh practice with targeted recovery.

Recovering a Total or Partner Share from a Difference asks you to decide what determines each person’s share or assigned amount. Use the difference between profit shares to find an unknown total, capital, or contribution. We will build the model from the agreement, calculate a representative case, and test the result against the original conditions.

Start with the quantity the agreement actually rewards. In ordinary partnership profit sharing, that is the capital made available to the business over time. A difference between two shares can determine the total when their ratio weights are known. Write the partner or user labels and the stated basis before you choose an operation.

The core model is: each partner’s weight = capital × time invested. This follows by comparing equal units of capital-month: twice the capital for the same duration contributes twice as much, and the same capital held twice as long also contributes twice as much.

If the two weights are a and b out of total W, their share difference is P·|a−b|/W. Solve for P only after confirming both shares use the same distributable pool. Keep the capital amount and its time period in separate columns first. Only multiply once the quantities use compatible units; this makes the origin of every ratio term visible.

Worked reasoning: With weights 46:35, the difference is 11 parts out of 81. If the share gap is ₹1,100, one part is ₹100 and the total profit is ₹8,100. Notice that the ratio comes from relative contribution, not from the order in which partners are named or from who manages the business. Preserve the labels until the final allocation.

When the total profit is known, add the reduced ratio terms to find total parts. Divide the distributable profit by those parts for one part, then multiply by the requested partner’s parts. Do not treat a ratio term itself as a rupee amount.

Use the timeline or agreement to identify intervals before doing arithmetic. Write each share as a fraction of P before taking their difference. If a partner’s capital changes, record the new amount only from the date it takes effect; if a time factor is common to everyone, cancel it only after forming the ratio.

A second way to check the model is to rebuild each partner’s contribution independently. Substitute the recovered total and compute both shares; their difference should reproduce the given amount. If the resulting ratio reverses a known relationship—for example, a larger weighted contribution receiving a smaller share—inspect the partner labels and ratio order.

Watch for this error: Do not subtract the ratio terms and call the result a money amount; it is only a number of parts. Another frequent slip is to use elapsed time instead of invested time. Mark the start and end of each interval; for a late entrant in a T-month business, invested duration is T minus the delay.

A useful worked check is to allocate the full pool and add the receipts. For partner i, the share is total profit × (i’s weight / all partners’ weights). This fraction must be between 0 and 1 for positive weights, and all partner fractions must sum to 1.

Translate special wording before calculation. A percentage increase may refer to original capital, a withdrawal may be partial, and an allowance may be removed before investment-based sharing. A difference between one partner’s capital and another’s is a separate condition and must not be confused with a difference in profit shares. Underline the base of each percentage and state whether the pool is original or remaining profit.

If an unknown amount or date is requested, set up the relationship before solving. Equate the capital-time products in the stated profit ratio, or write a share as its fraction of total profit. Keep unknowns tied to their partner labels and check that a date remains within the business term.

If your first answer seems wrong, revisit the model rather than repeating the arithmetic. Ask: did I use the right basis, include every interval, convert all time units, and use the right total pool? Then substitute the candidate into the original data and recompute the ratio.

For a timed exam, use a compact ledger: partner; capital in each interval; months in that interval; weighted contribution; share fraction. Reduce large products by common factors only after they are formed, and keep exact fractions until the final currency amount.

Mastery check: explain why the chosen weights represent the agreement, show one intermediate calculation, and verify the final share or sufficiency conclusion. You should now be able to solve the approved scope for recovering a total or partner share from a difference without relying on a memorized answer pattern.

Model the named partners and the profit pool before calculating. The share gap corresponds to the difference of their ratio parts, not the total number of parts. Keep every capital, duration, and change attached to its partner.
Two partners’ capital-time weights are in the ratio 46:35. Their profit shares differ by ₹1100. Find the total profit.

inlineData.prompt: Two partners’ capital-time weights are in the ratio 46:35. Their profit shares differ by ₹1100. Find the total profit.
hints: The share gap corresponds to the difference of their ratio parts, not the total number of parts.
inlineData.explanation: The share difference is |46−35|=11 parts out of 81. Thus 11/81 of total profit equals ₹1100. Total=₹1100×81/11=₹8100.

content.text: Let’s repair the specific idea: The share gap corresponds to the difference of their ratio parts, not the total number of parts. Set gap/total=|46−35|/(46+35).
